Protocols, Units of Account & Custody

Sixteen Hours Is Not a Week: When Layer-2 Speeds Up, Timelocks Shrink and Custody Re-Prices

Base flips its block cadence tenfold without consent, shortening seven-day timelocks into sixteen hours; Zcash itemizes its emission curve to eight decimal places; and a central bank intervention in Paraguay locks three million out of their accounts.

When protocol architects confuse an ordinal block height with an immutable calendar, the arithmetic of downstream contracts quietly disintegrates [s540]. On Thursday, Coinbase’s Layer-2 network Base minted block 53,556,127 just two seconds after block 53,556,126, activating its Denim upgrade and shifting its block target from two seconds down to two hundred milliseconds [s540]. The operational reality was instantaneous and severe: every smart contract on Base that counts time in blocks began ticking ten times faster [s540].

As researcher Roger observed, an immutable timelock configured for 302,400 blocks—traditionally glossed as one week of safety—instantly shrank to sixteen hours and forty-eight minutes [s540]. Base’s own technical specification noted without euphemism that any system that treats a block count as a duration will see that duration shrink to one tenth of its intended length after activation. [s540]. Layer-3 deployment Horizen found itself permanently unable to process user transactions within forty minutes of activation, its DAO forced to return assets to holders on Base [s540]. Describing the failure mode, Roger observed that a unit of account drifted while every promise denominated in it silently repriced [s540].

The contrast across the ecosystem was striking [s540]. The same evening, Zcash activated its NU7 upgrade, cutting block times from 75 to 25 seconds [s540]. Yet ZIP 218 adjusted the halving interval from 1,680,000 to 5,040,000 blocks and itemized that three post-upgrade blocks produce precisely one zatoshi less than one pre-upgrade block, calculating that the 25-second chain falls short of its 21-million cap by exactly 0.68062995 ZEC across its entire remaining lifespan [s540]. Contrasting the engineering disciplines, Roger pointed out that while Zcash calculated what the emission curve becomes to the eighth decimal place, Base changed its constant without an inventory of affected contracts [s540].

Outside blockchains, the fragility of institutional custody was underscored in Asuncion, Paraguay, where the central bank moved to resolve Ueno Bank after its solvency ratio collapsed [s540]. Approximately three million depositors—exceeding 60 percent of adults in the nation—awoke to frozen debit cards, disabled apps, and riot police deployed outside branches [s23, s540]. Fitch had maintained a "BB" solvency rating on the institution as recently as March [s540]. As Coincards.com observed from the sidelines: One day your bank says your savings are safe. The next day: app gone, cards gone, life savings frozen, and you're waiting on a central bank payout schedule to get a slice back. [s66].

The Dispatch & Engineering Wire
Exchange Infrastructure

Payjoin Goes Default at Bull Bitcoin

Bull Bitcoin announced that every on-chain buy and sell executed through its mobile wallet now defaults to Payjoin transactions without requiring user configuration [s18]. The exchange, which has collaborated with the Payjoin Foundation since late 2024, aims to break standard clustering assumptions made by blockchain analytics firms while consolidating UTXOs to lower future mempool fees [s18].

Elsewhere, developer Tidwell published proposals for Tuliproot, an identity key rotation framework designed to offer backward compatibility with Nostr npubs while addressing the mempool trust gap between broadcast and confirmation [s6, s20].

Software Releases

Mullvad Browser 16.0 Ships AArch64 and quad9

Mullvad released version 16.0 of its privacy browser, rebased on Firefox ESR 153 [s8]. The build introduces generic window titles to prevent local host applications from snooping on tab activity, adds a dedicated Clear Private Session control, switches default encrypted DNS to Quad9, and introduces native Linux ARM (AArch64) support for Apple Silicon and Raspberry Pi hardware [s8].

In client utilities, Mostro debuted Mostro World, an open explorer mapping live peer-to-peer orders, dispute resolutions, and volume distributions without tracker scripts or user accounts [s13]. Meanwhile, Freedom.Tech tracked forty routine software updates alongside security patches in AdGuard Home and Caddy [s536].

Relay Conformance & Hardware

Auditing NIP-01 and Hardware Integrity

Relay operator relayted.de published an implementation audit guide urging server administrators to verify NIP-01 conformance against synthetic deterministic datasets rather than trusting defaults [s539]. Crucially, the analysis warns against honoring NIP-09 deletion events signed by unauthorized third parties [s539].

Hardware wallet maker Foundation published its post-mortem covering an October email security breach, reassuring users that firmware architecture ensures keys held on Passport hardware were never exposed [s26].
